newsitem.title: UK: WHO asks world leaders to unite against TB.
newsitem.headline: WHO asks world leaders to unite against TB.

text.p: The World Health Organisation (WHO) called on world leaders on Friday to back its new strategy to treat the deadly lung disease tuberculosis or face a worldwide epidemic.

The WHO said the number of tuberculosis (TB) cases could fall rapidly if its new strategy, DOTS -- the Directly Observed Treatment, Short-course -- was used to treat seven out of every 10 patients, instead of the current one out of 10.

"The World Health Organisation calls on political and community leaders, medical and health officials, doctors and nurses, to use DOTS more widely," Dr Hiroshi Nakajima, Director-General of the WHO told a news conference.
The WHO said DOTS could cost just $100 per patient for an entire course of treatment but said investment was needed to get the strategy up and running.

DOTS seeks to train community members to ensure patients take their six-month course of antibiotics until they are completely cured, with "default chasers" tracking down those who lapse. This combats the development of drug resistance which develops when a patient does not take a full course of drugs.
Sir John Crofton, Professor Emeritus at the University of Edinburgh said that if world leaders failed to take notice of the call for wider use of the strategy, the consequences could be disastrous.
"If they fail to do that then -- with the HIV epidemic and the bad inefficent treatment that occurs without DOTS -- these (poorer) countries are likely to get an epidemic."
HIV sufferers are prone to fall foul of TB due to their weakened immune system and, while they can be treated for TB, their life expectancy is reduced after after recovering from TB.
Crofton sighted ignorance, carelessness and complacency amongst doctors in poorer countries as having increased multi-drug resistence.

He said drug resistance had grown because doctors in poorer countries had prescribed their patients inappropriate drug combinations, with the added problem that patients could often not afford to pay for the drugs.
Patients who are drug resistant can be cured, the WHO said, but at a cost of $250,000, an impracticable amount in poor countries.

Tuberculosis still ravages the world's poorer nations, particularly in Africa, the Indian subcontinent and now in eastern Europe, with eight to 10 million people currently suffering from the disease worldwide.
Though the WHO's message was largely directed at combating TB in these poor countries, it said the West was also at risk.
"When you get a TB-infected person who gets on a jumbo jet, they reckon everyone within eight rows of the patient can be at risk," said Crofton.
